title: Malted brown loaf
subtitle: British granary-style tin loaf with malt flakes
excerpt: Malted brown loaf is a British tin bread made with brown or granary flour and added malt extract for depth of flavour. It has a medium crumb, a soft crust from the tin, and a slightly sweet, nutty taste. The malt extract accelerates the yeast, so watch the prove carefully.
sourceNotes:
- British granary bread tradition (documented in various public-domain baking manuals)
- Flour Advisory Bureau historical records on malted wheat flour
- Elizabeth David, English Bread and Yeast Cookery (1977)

glossaryTerms.definition: The rest of shaped dough before baking, during which yeast produces gas that expands the loaf. The dough is ready when it has increased noticeably in volume and springs back slowly when pressed.
The process by which flour proteins bond into elastic strands when mixed with water. Adequate gluten development gives bread structure and allows the dough to trap gas produced by yeast.

recipe.freezeNotes: Slice and freeze for up to 2 months.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The dough can be mixed the evening before and proved in the refrigerator overnight; shape and bake the next morning.

baking.bakeTemperatureNote: conventional oven; reduce to 200°C after 10 minutes
baking.steamMethod: No steam required for a tin loaf

content.text: Malted brown loaf is a British tin bread with a medium crumb and a soft, slightly sticky crust. You get a mellow, nutty sweetness from the malt extract and a satisfying chew from the brown flour. Malt extract feeds the yeast faster than sugar does, so the
prove
is shorter than a standard white tin loaf and needs watching.

attrs.prepNote: liquid or paste; warm briefly in the microwave if very thick
optional; stir in with the flour for texture

content.text: Method
Mix the dough

Weigh the brown bread flour and strong white flour into a large mixing bowl. If using malted wheat flakes, add them now and stir through the flour. Add the salt to one side of the bowl and the dried yeast to the other.

Stir the malt extract into the warm water until dissolved (it does not need to dissolve completely; it will incorporate in the dough). Add the oil. Pour the liquid into the flour and mix with your hand or a silicone spatula until no dry flour remains. The dough will be slightly stickier than a white tin loaf dough: the bran in the brown flour absorbs water more slowly.
Knead
Turn the dough onto a lightly floured surface and knead for 10 minutes by hand. Good
gluten development

is what gives the loaf structure. Wholegrain particles in the brown flour will cut through forming gluten strands; this is normal and is why the 10% strong white flour is included to give the network more support.
The dough is ready when it is smooth and springs back when you press it with a finger. It will never be as silky as a white dough: a slightly rougher surface from the bran particles is correct.
Shape into a ball, return to the bowl, and cover with a damp cloth. Leave in a warm place for 60 minutes, or until roughly doubled in size.
Shape and prove

Lightly grease a 900 g loaf tin. Tip the dough onto a lightly floured surface. Press it gently into a rectangle about the length of the tin. Roll the rectangle up firmly from one short end, pinch the seam, and place seam-side down in the tin.
Cover loosely and leave to
prove

for 45 minutes. Because the malt extract accelerates the yeast, check after 35 minutes. The loaf is ready when it crowns just above the tin rim and a finger prod leaves an indent that fills back in slowly.
Bake
Heat the oven to 220°C conventional. Place the loaf tin in the centre of the oven and bake for 10 minutes.
After 10 minutes, reduce the oven temperature to 200°C and bake for a further 25 minutes. The malt extract darkens faster than plain dough: the crust will be a deep mahogany colour, which is correct.
Turn the loaf out and tap the base: it should sound hollow. If not, return to the oven directly on the rack for 5 more minutes. Cool fully on a wire rack before slicing.

attrs.problem: Loaf over-proved and collapsed in the oven
attrs.avoid: Avoid relying only on the clock: malt extract speeds up the yeast, particularly in a warm kitchen. Check the dough at 35 minutes rather than waiting the full 45.

attrs.problem: Crust very dark but inside under-baked
attrs.avoid: Avoid judging doneness by crust colour alone with a malted loaf. The malt sugars brown faster than plain dough. Always confirm with the hollow-tap test on the base.
Avoid under-kneading. Brown flour needs a full 10 minutes to develop enough gluten to support the loaf. A finger-poke test on the kneaded dough should show a slow, definite spring-back.

attrs.problem: Malt extract lumpy and not incorporating
attrs.avoid: Avoid adding cold, very thick malt extract straight from the jar. Warm it briefly (10 seconds in the microwave or stand the jar in hot water) so it loosens enough to stir into the water.
